title: India Is About to Tokenize Its Corporate Bond Market. SEBI Just Launched a Blockchain Pilot That Could Let NRIs Buy Indian Debt the Way They Buy Stocks.
excerpt: The pilot will test near-instant settlement, automated servicing, and full traceability for corporate bonds. India's ₹59 lakh crore bond market has less household awareness than cryptocurrency. SEBI wants to change that.
body:
India's Securities and Exchange Board just took the most concrete step any Indian financial regulator has ever taken toward putting blockchain technology inside the plumbing of the country's capital markets.

At the CareEdge Debt Market Summit 2026 in Mumbai on Tuesday, SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey announced that the regulator has formally decided to launch a pilot project for tokenising corporate bonds using distributed ledger technology. The timeline: six to nine months. The scope: limited to start, but designed to test whether DLT can do for India's bond market what UPI did for payments — make it faster, cheaper, and accessible to people who never thought of using it.

## What Tokenisation Actually Means

Tokenisation converts a corporate bond — traditionally a paper or digital certificate held in a depository account — into a digital token recorded on a distributed ledger. Instead of settlement cycles that take one to two days through intermediaries, tokenised bonds can settle near-instantly. Every transaction is traceable. Coupon payments and maturity redemptions can be automated through smart contracts.

"Once you do that, there will be a greater possibility of more liquidity and instantaneous autonomous settlements," Pandey told reporters at the event.

SEBI wants the pilot to evaluate four specific outcomes: faster settlement, improved traceability, automated debt servicing, and greater transparency for all market participants. Pandey was careful to clarify that this is not a replacement for existing infrastructure but an exploration of whether DLT can add efficiency on top of it.

## Why India's Bond Market Needs This

India's corporate bond market has grown from ₹17.5 lakh crore at the end of FY15 to over ₹59 lakh crore today — a compound annual growth rate of approximately 12 percent. In FY26 alone, debt issuances mobilised ₹9.1 lakh crore, nearly twice the amount raised through equity markets.

But scale has not translated into depth. The secondary market for corporate bonds remains thin. Retail participation is almost nonexistent. And here is the statistic that should make every financial regulator in India uncomfortable: according to SEBI's own investor survey, awareness of corporate bonds as an investment product stands at just 10 percent — lower than cryptocurrency awareness at 15 percent.

Household penetration of corporate bonds is below 1 percent.

The irony is difficult to overstate. Corporate bonds issued by India's largest companies, regulated by SEBI, with predictable cash flows and lower volatility than equities, have less name recognition among Indian households than an asset class the government taxes at 30 percent flat and has repeatedly warned citizens about.

## What This Could Mean for NRIs

For non-resident Indians who have been wary of Indian debt markets — put off by opaque pricing, slow settlement, and limited access through NRE/NRO accounts — tokenisation could be transformative.

Today, if an NRI wants to buy an Indian corporate bond, the process involves a broker, a depository participant, a demat account linked to the right type of bank account, and settlement that takes T+1 or T+2 days. The friction is high enough that most NRIs who want fixed-income exposure to India default to FD rates at SBI or HDFC, leaving significant yield on the table.

A tokenised bond market, if designed with cross-border participation in mind, could collapse that friction. Near-instant settlement. Transparent pricing on a shared ledger. Fractional ownership that lowers the minimum investment from ₹10 lakh to something a salaried NRI can afford.

SEBI has not yet confirmed whether the pilot will include provisions for NRI participation. But the direction is clear — and the Reserve Bank of India's parallel work on NRI deposit schemes and dollar mobilisation (currently under review after the rupee fell to a record 96.96 per dollar last week) suggests that Delhi is thinking hard about how to channel diaspora capital into Indian markets.

## The Broader Market Context

Pandey's announcement came on the same day that Taiwan's stock market overtook India's by market capitalisation — $4.95 trillion versus $4.92 trillion. The SEBI Chairman addressed it directly: "India is a very diversified market. In Taiwan, there are concentrated stocks," he said, noting that global AI-driven investment flows are inflating valuations in semiconductor-heavy markets.

The Indian equity market tells a split story in 2026. The Nifty 50 and Sensex are down 8.3 percent and 10.5 percent year-to-date, battered by the Iran war energy shock and relentless foreign selling. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled $23.86 billion from Indian stocks so far this year — surpassing all of last year's record outflows. Bank of America has warned that foreign investors are unlikely to return to India before 2027 or even 2028.

But small-caps and mid-caps have gained 2.6 and 2.2 percent respectively. Brokerages are projecting that June will be a "stock-pickers' market" — selective, sector-specific, and driven by domestic money rather than foreign flows.

For NRIs evaluating where to deploy capital in India, the message is nuanced: equities are in a correction driven by foreign exits, debt markets are on the cusp of structural modernisation, and the rupee — now considered undervalued by the RBI governor himself — could appreciate once the West Asia situation normalises.

## The Quantum Risk SEBI Is Already Thinking About

In a notable aside, Pandey flagged quantum computing as a risk to blockchain-based financial infrastructure. "We must move carefully, but we must remain open to useful innovation," he said.

The concern is real: quantum computers could eventually break the cryptographic algorithms that secure distributed ledger systems. But the timeline for that threat is measured in years, not months — and the settlement improvements from tokenisation are available now.

SEBI's willingness to acknowledge the risk while proceeding with the pilot suggests a regulatory maturity that the Indian financial system has not always displayed. For once, the regulator is ahead of the market, not behind it.

"The corporate bond market is the economy's second engine of credit," Pandey said. "It reduces over-reliance on banks. A deep bond market can finance infrastructure, productive capacity, urbanisation, energy transition, housing, logistics, and digital infrastructure."

For the 32 million NRIs worldwide who have been sending money to India but rarely investing it in Indian debt, SEBI is building a door that might actually be worth walking through.
author: Diaspora Desk
